identification.summary: Leopard Typhoon is Microsoft's name for a China-origin actor formerly tracked by Microsoft as LEAD [S1]. Microsoft maps WICKED PANDA, TG-2633, TG-3279, Mana, KAOS, Red Diablo and Winnti Group to it [S1]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the actor as Winnti Group (G0044). MITRE describes a group with Chinese origins, active since at least 2010, that heavily targeted the gaming industry and has since widened its targeting [S2]. In its January 2017 post on German industrial attacks, Microsoft described how Windows Defender ATP flags Winnti-related activity by the LEAD and BARIUM activity groups [S3]. Microsoft described LEAD as the industrial-espionage group that steals code-signing certificates to sign its malware [S3].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2010 [S2]. Kaspersky first publicly reported the group in 2013 [S8].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Leopard Typhoon (legacy element name LEAD) [S1]. MITRE match: Winnti Group (G0044) [S2]. Cluster boundary caution: Microsoft separates LEAD from BARIUM (now Brass Typhoon), describing BARIUM as focused on electronic gaming, multimedia and internet content and using social-media rapport and malicious macro, .chm or .lnk first stages [S3]. Microsoft also lists WICKED PANDA under both Leopard Typhoon and Brass Typhoon [S1]. Several vendors do not draw this line. Symantec groups Winnti, APT41, Barium, Blackfly and Wicked Panda together [S9]. LAC's RevivalStone reporting is covered as 'Winnti (APT41)' and overlaps Trend Micro's Earth Freybug, an APT41 subset [S10]. 'Winnti' is also a malware family name used by several groups [S2]. Reports titled 'Winnti' may therefore describe Brass Typhoon activity rather than Leopard Typhoon.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (origin per Microsoft's naming mapping) [S1]. German public broadcaster ARD reported in 2019 that analysis of Winnti code pointed to a group likely working for the Chinese government [S7].
attribution.confidence: No Microsoft confidence statement on state sponsorship of Leopard Typhoon was found; Microsoft assigns China as the origin [S1]. MITRE describes Chinese origins [S2]. In 2019, a DCSO executive said 'we can assume that there is a very targeted tasking by the Chinese state,' while noting definite proof was impossible [S6]. That statement concerns Winnti intrusions in Germany and is not a government attribution. No US government indictment, advisory or sanction naming Leopard Typhoon or LEAD was found in this research.
attribution.basis: Microsoft naming mapping and 2017 Windows Defender ATP reporting [S1][S3]; MITRE ATT&CK group record [S2]; vendor reporting from ESET, Symantec and LAC [S4][S5][S9][S10]; German press investigations reported by AFP and Reuters [S6][S7].

objectives: Industrial and commercial espionage. A threat-actor card summarizing Microsoft's 2017 reporting says LEAD sought research materials, process documents and project plans [S11]. Microsoft said LEAD steals code-signing certificates and uses them to sign its malware in later attacks [S3]. Supply-chain compromise of software and game developers supports both espionage and onward access [S4][S5]. ESET found a cryptominer as the final payload of the 2019 gaming supply-chain attack and said a financial motive could not be ruled out [S4].

sectors: Online and video game developers and publishers [S2][S4][S5]
Materials and energy (Winnti/APT41-labeled reporting; boundary unclear) [S9][S10]
regions: South Korea and Taiwan (2020 game developers) [S5]
Thailand and wider Asia (2019 gaming supply chain; small numbers in Brazil, Peru, Turkey and Russia) [S4]
Switzerland (Roche) and other multinationals named by ARD, including Marriott, Lion Air, Sumitomo and Shin-Etsu [S7]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's 2017 post addresses German industrial victims [S3]. Victim lists from 2019 German press reporting attribute infections to 'Winnti' malware, not to a Microsoft-named cluster [S6][S7]. Materials, energy and Japan targeting comes from vendors that merge Winnti with APT41, so it may belong to Brass Typhoon under Microsoft's taxonomy [S9][S10].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft said LEAD uses Winnti malware for long-term access and signs malware with stolen code-signing certificates [S3]. A threat-actor card summarizing the same reporting says initial access typically came from emailed Winnti installers, with brute-forced logins, SQL injection and unpatched web servers also used [S11]. MITRE attributes Winnti for Windows, PlugX and PipeMon to the group [S2]. ESET reported supply-chain compromise of game developers' build environments, so that malware shipped inside legitimate software. ESET also reported the PortReuse backdoor and continued use of ShadowPad variants [S4]. In 2020, ESET reported the modular PipeMon backdoor, which persisted as a Print Processor and was signed with a likely stolen certificate. In one case the actor reached a build orchestration server [S5]. Winnti/APT41-labeled reporting from 2023-2025 describes the Winnkit backdoor and heavier use of open-source tools [S9]. It also describes ERP SQL injection, China Chopper and Behinder web shells, abuse of a maintenance provider's shared account, and a 'Winnti v5.0' RAT with rootkit and loader [S10][S12].

campaigns.name: Kaspersky exposure of Winnti
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky first publicly reported the Winnti group in 2013. Security Affairs says the researchers assessed it as active since 2007.

campaigns.name: German conglomerate intrusion
campaigns.summary: Microsoft cited German press reports that intruders used Winnti as their main implant to keep access to a conglomerate's network from February 2016. Reuters, citing media reports at the time, describes a 2016 Winnti attack on ThyssenKrupp.

campaigns.name: Microsoft LEAD/BARIUM reporting
campaigns.summary: Microsoft described how Windows Defender ATP detects LEAD and BARIUM activity linked to Winnti in German industrial attacks, and separated LEAD (industrial espionage, certificate theft) from BARIUM (gaming and media).

campaigns.name: Bayer intrusion
campaigns.summary: Bayer confirmed in April 2019 that it detected Winnti infections in early 2018 and cleaned up the systems with DCSO and North Rhine-Westphalia police. Bayer said no data was stolen.

campaigns.name: Asian gaming supply-chain attacks
campaigns.summary: ESET reported compromised game builds distributing malware, with victims concentrated in Thailand and Asia and a custom XMRig miner as the final payload.

campaigns.name: German DAX and multinational victims (ARD)
campaigns.summary: ARD reported Winnti infections. Siemens, Henkel and Roche confirmed they were affected by Winnti; BASF and Covestro confirmed only that they had been attacked. All said no sensitive information was lost.

campaigns.name: PortReuse and ShadowPad arsenal (ESET)
campaigns.summary: ESET documented the PortReuse backdoor and active ShadowPad variants, and warned an Asian mobile hardware and software manufacturer that it was compromised.

campaigns.name: PipeMon against Korean and Taiwanese game developers
campaigns.summary: ESET found the PipeMon backdoor at MMO developers in South Korea and Taiwan, linked to Winnti by shared C2 domains. The actor reached a build orchestration server in at least one case.

campaigns.name: Operation CuckooBees (overlapping cluster)
campaigns.summary: Cybereason reporting, as covered by Dark Reading, describes Winnti theft of trade secrets from technology and manufacturing companies. Attribution is shared with APT41/BARIUM.

campaigns.name: Blackfly against materials sector (overlapping cluster)
campaigns.summary: Symantec reported Blackfly targeting two subsidiaries of an Asian conglomerate in materials and composites in late 2022 to early 2023, using Winnkit and open-source tools.

campaigns.name: RevivalStone (overlapping cluster)
campaigns.summary: LAC reported, as covered in February 2025, Winnti intrusions into Japanese manufacturing, materials and energy firms. Access came through ERP SQL injection and spread through a maintenance provider to three more organizations.

diamond.adversary: China-origin actor that Microsoft calls Leopard Typhoon (formerly LEAD) [S1][S3]. MITRE tracks it as Winnti Group (G0044) [S2]. Several vendors fold it into APT41 [S9][S10].
diamond.capability: Winnti RAT and rootkit, PlugX, PipeMon, PortReuse and ShadowPad; malware signed with stolen certificates; software supply-chain tampering [S2][S3][S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 domains reused across campaigns, which ESET used to link PipeMon to Winnti [S5]; compromised developer build environments and build orchestration servers [S4][S5]; a trusted maintenance provider's shared account (RevivalStone) [S10].
diamond.victim: Game developers and players in Asia [S4][S5]; German industrial, chemical and pharmaceutical multinationals [S3][S6][S7]; Asian hardware manufacturers [S4]; Japanese manufacturing, materials and energy firms (overlapping cluster) [S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: German commentators linked the targeting to China's economic goals, and DCSO suggested Chinese state tasking [S6]. Intellectual property and certificate theft support commercial and technology advancement [S3][S11].
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise networks, code-signing trust, software build pipelines, internet-facing ERP and web applications, and outsourced IT maintenance relationships [S3][S4][S5][S10].

gaps: Microsoft has not published a profile under the name Leopard Typhoon that could be found. Microsoft's 2017 LEAD post was seen only as a search result and could not be fetched (DNS failure), so its details here come from search summaries and the ETDA card [S3][S11].

The boundary between Leopard Typhoon (LEAD) and Brass Typhoon (BARIUM/APT41) is unresolved. Microsoft separates them, but Symantec, LAC and others merge 'Winnti' with APT41. CuckooBees, Blackfly and RevivalStone are recorded as overlapping clusters, not confirmed Leopard Typhoon activity [S1][S3][S9][S10].
German 2019 victim reporting attributes infections to Winnti malware, which several groups share. Which Microsoft cluster was responsible is not stated [S2][S7].

Primary vendor reports were not opened because WebFetch could not resolve the hosts: ESET white papers, Symantec Blackfly, LAC RevivalStone, Cybereason CuckooBees, and Kaspersky 2013/2015. Content comes from search summaries and press coverage.
No US government indictment, advisory or sanction naming Leopard Typhoon or LEAD was found. The September 2020 DOJ APT41 indictments concern Wicked Panda/APT41 and were not reviewed for this record.
Microsoft maps the names TG-2633, TG-3279, Mana, KAOS and Red Diablo to Leopard Typhoon, but their originating reports were not identified [S1].
No reporting from 2025-2026 specific to Leopard Typhoon was found; the most recent Winnti-labeled activity found is the 2024 RevivalStone campaign [S10][S12].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1 (operational environment): the relevant terrain is commercial software and game build pipelines, code-signing infrastructure, internet-facing ERP and web servers, outsourced IT maintenance accounts, and industrial, chemical and pharmaceutical R&D networks [S3][S4][S5][S10]. Defense-industrial-base suppliers fall within this terrain. Step 2 (effects): signed malware and trojanized legitimate software weaken signature-based trust. Long dwell times, such as Bayer detecting infections in early 2018 that were disclosed in 2019, show durable access [S3][S4][S6]. Step 3 (adversary template): initial access by phishing a Winnti installer, web or SQL injection, or a supply-chain compromise. Persistence follows through Winnti RAT and rootkit, PipeMon or ShadowPad, then lateral movement through shared or provider accounts and theft of documents and certificates [S4][S5][S10][S11]. Step 4: the MLCOA is continued IP and certificate theft from manufacturing, materials and technology firms in Asia and Europe [S3][S7][S9][S10]. The MDCOA is the use of stolen signing certificates or a compromised build server to push trojanized updates into software DoD or its suppliers use. This is inferred from the 2019-2020 supply-chain activity; no documented campaign against DoD exists [S4][S5]. Candidate indicators: binaries signed with certificates from unrelated vendors; unexpected Print Processor registrations; new web shells (China Chopper, Behinder) on ERP or web servers; anomalous use of maintenance-provider shared accounts; DNS to C2 domains reused from prior Winnti campaigns [S5][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track certificate revocations, vendor and game-studio supply-chain compromises, and Winnti, PipeMon and ShadowPad detections. Account for shared Winnti malware when attributing [S2][S4][S5]. Authorities: observed victims are almost entirely private-sector firms in Germany, Japan and Asia, so DoD action toward exposed suppliers would normally run through DC3 and DIB partnership and interagency channels, not direct DODIN operations [S6][S7][S10]. Mission assurance: the main DODIN risk is trust in signed third-party software and managed-service accounts. Prioritize allow-listing that does not rely on signature alone, and monitor provider access [S3][S10]. Coordination: deconflict with partners that track Brass Typhoon/APT41, since vendors merge the clusters, and with allied CERTs such as Germany's and Japan's, which have handled Winnti cases [S1][S6][S9][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: Winnti Group is a threat group with Chinese origins that has been active since at least 2010. The group has heavily targeted the gaming industry, but it has also expanded the scope of its targeting. Some reporting suggests a number of other groups, including Axiom, APT17, and Ke3chang, are closely linked to Winnti Group.
